speaker: Chelsea Finn
title: No Priors Ep. 107 | With Physical Intelligence Co-Founder Chelsea Finn
question: Why does real-world deployment pose a fundamentally different error-tolerance challenge for robotics than for typical machine learning applications?
guest: I think one thing that's actually challenging is that typically in machine learning, for a lot of the successful applications like recommender systems, language models, and image detection, the consumers of the model outputs are actually humans who can check it, and the humans are good at checking it. A lot of the very natural applications of robots involve the robot doing something autonomously on its own, where it's not like a human is consuming the commanded arm position, checking it, and validating it. So I think we need to think about new ways of having some kind of tolerance for mistakes, or scenarios where that's fine, or scenarios where humans and robots can work together. That's one big challenge that will come up when trying to actually deploy these. Some of the language interaction work that we've been doing is actually motivated by this challenge, where we think it's really important for humans to be able to provide input for how they want the robot to behave, what they want the robot to do, and how they want the robot to help in a particular scenario.

points.core: Most successful ML products rely on humans to verify model outputs.
points.note: Accept: recommender systems, LLMs, or vision tools outputting predictions or text that human users easily inspect, filter, or catch errors on. Do not credit: generic claims that LLMs hallucinate without explaining the human verification loop.

points.core: Autonomous robots execute low-level motor commands without human pre-execution validation.
points.note: Accept: humans cannot inspect or approve each commanded joint or arm trajectory before physical execution, removing the human error buffer. Do not credit: vague mentions of safety risks without contrasting autonomous motor execution against human output review.

points.core: Viable early deployments target physical settings with built-in tolerance for mistakes.
points.note: Accept: choosing environments or tasks where occasional manipulation failures are benign, recoverable, or low-cost. Do not credit: generic advice to start small.

points.core: Interactive human-in-the-loop steering helps compensate for imperfect autonomous robot execution.
points.note: Accept: language-guided feedback, human-robot collaboration, or allowing users to direct and correct robot behavior mid-task. Do not credit: generic mentions of human-in-the-loop without connecting it to managing robot error tolerance.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Robotics differs because its errors are physical, compounding, and often irreversible, whereas most machine learning applications produce errors that are informational, isolated, and cheap to correct.

When a recommender, translator, or chatbot makes a mistake, the result is a bad output that a human can ignore, filter, or retry. A system that is right 95% of the time is often still useful. A robot's mistake, by contrast, acts on the world: it can break objects, damage itself, or injure people, and there is no undo.

Robots also operate in closed loop over long sequences of actions. Each action changes the state the robot sees next, so small errors push it into situations unlike its training data, where further errors become more likely. Per-step reliability therefore multiplies: a task with 100 steps at 99% success each completes only about a third of the time.

Finally, the physical world presents an endless long tail of unusual situations, and there is typically no human in the loop to catch failures in real time. Useful deployment thus demands reliability far above what typical ML benchmarks reward.

points.why: The response identifies human filtering and correction as a buffer against errors in common ML products.
quotes: When a recommender, translator, or chatbot makes a mistake, the result is a bad output that a human can ignore, filter, or retry.

The response calls for higher reliability and gives no strategy for choosing settings where mistakes are benign or recoverable.
The response gives no mechanism for people to steer or correct robot behavior to manage execution errors.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Typical machine learning applications operate in digital environments where predictions are isolated and errors carry low, reversible costs; a misclassified image or flawed recommendation rarely alters the underlying world and can easily be corrected or ignored. Robotics, by contrast, couples perception directly to physical action, fundamentally changing what error tolerance requires. First, physical failures are immediate and irreversible: a brief miscalculation can damage hardware, break objects, or injure people, making worst-case safety guarantees far more critical than high average accuracy. Second, robots operate in sequential closed loops rather than on independent, identically distributed inputs. Because every action changes the physical environment and future sensor readings, small errors push the robot into unfamiliar, out-of-distribution states where mistakes rapidly compound over time. Finally, real-world physics imposes strict real-time deadlines amid noisy sensors, partial observability, and unpredictable surroundings, meaning a moving robot cannot simply pause, abstain, or retry when uncertain, and must remain safe across the long tail of rare edge cases.

points.why: The response says digital errors are easy to correct or ignore but never identifies human review as the mechanism that catches them.
The response links perception to physical action but never explains that autonomous robots execute motor commands without prior human validation.
The response emphasizes worst-case safety without proposing early deployment in settings where occasional mistakes are benign or recoverable.
The response gives no role to human guidance or correction in managing errors during robot operation.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: Typical machine learning applications, such as recommendation, search, translation, or chatbots, run in a forgiving loop. Each prediction is cheap and usually reversible, and a human often reviews the output. A wrong answer costs a bad click or a quick retry, so a system that is right 90–95% of the time can still be very useful. Robots act physically, so their errors happen in the world and often can't be undone. A dropped object, a collision, or an injured person can't be retried. Robot errors also compound: each action changes what the robot sees next, so a small mistake can push it into states its training data never covered, and the errors cascade. That's the familiar distribution-shift problem in imitation learning. Long tasks with many steps multiply per-step failure rates. A policy that's 99% reliable per step fails often across hundreds of steps. Deployment also happens in open, messy settings with rare edge cases, and often without anyone supervising. Robotics therefore needs reliability near "five nines" plus safe recovery from failures, a much higher bar than the "usually right" standard most ML products meet.

points.why: The response identifies human review and easy retries as reasons typical ML products can tolerate wrong outputs.
quotes: a human often reviews the output
A wrong answer costs a bad click or a quick retry

points.why: The response mentions unsupervised deployment but leaves out the absence of human checks on individual motor commands before execution.
The response calls for safe recovery but does not propose choosing tasks or settings where occasional physical mistakes are tolerable.
The response does not describe humans steering or correcting robot behavior to manage execution errors.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: In typical machine learning applications such as search, recommendations, or text generation, predictions are largely independent and mistakes are cheap, reversible, and isolated. Robotics operates under fundamentally different conditions because robots act in a closed physical loop. Every action changes the environment and shapes future observations, so a small mistake does not remain isolated; it compounds over time and pushes the system into unfamiliar states far outside its training distribution. Even a model with high per-step accuracy can fail reliably over long horizons when minor errors accumulate across hundreds of continuous control steps. Furthermore, physical errors carry irreversible, high-stakes consequences: a single bad decision can break hardware, damage surroundings, or injure people, meaning rare tail-end failures that are tolerable in software become unacceptable in deployment. Finally, robots must handle unpredictable real-world dynamics under strict real-time latency constraints, with no simple way to pause, retry, or undo an action once momentum and gravity take over.

points.why: The response attributes ML error tolerance to cheap, reversible, isolated mistakes and omits human review of model outputs.
The response describes closed-loop physical execution but omits the absence of human review before individual motor commands are executed.
The response emphasizes the costs of physical errors without proposing deployment in settings where occasional failures are benign or recoverable.
The response does not describe how users could steer or correct robot behavior to compensate for execution errors.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A robot’s errors can change the physical world before anyone has a chance to correct them. A bad recommendation can often be ignored or revised. A robot that misjudges how close a person is may hit them before it can recover. Its actions also determine what happens next, so a small mistake can put it in an unfamiliar situation and trigger further errors.

That makes average accuracy an incomplete measure of readiness. A rare failure can become likely over thousands of hours of operation, and its consequences can outweigh many successful runs. Real-world robots therefore need to detect uncertainty and recover safely or stop before an error causes harm.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer: In many machine learning applications, a wrong prediction is easy to correct or ignore. A robot’s prediction can immediately become a physical action. If it misjudges the distance to a person and moves, a correct estimate a moment later may come too late to prevent injury. Each action also changes the conditions for the next decision, so a small error can compound. High average accuracy therefore tells only part of the story. A deployed robot must also recognize when it is uncertain and be able to slow down, stop, or recover before an error causes harm.
